headline: Trolled the Elbow at sunrise, anchored on the break after dark — yellowfin, a bigeye, and one green-lit wahoo to show for it
subhead: Stable weather let us run deep and stay out; the fish rewarded patience more than horsepower this week.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday night looking at the fuel burn and the forecast: run the 82 miles to Wilmington, troll the edge from first light until the sun got high, then sit on anchor and chunk through the evening bite instead of running home. With gas the way it is, you don't burn diesel twice in a day chasing a maybe. Calm seas and light out of the southwest meant we could commit to the long day without worrying about getting bounced around on the way back, so we took it.

We picked up the warm filament coming off the Stream right where it always seems to set up this time of year — pushing up over the canyon edge around the Elbow, 38°45' north, 72°28' west, with the color change and a hard temp break where the water jumped a couple degrees inside a half mile. That's the kind of seam that stacks bait, and it did. Flying fish everywhere, a few scattered patches of weed holding small mahi, and enough surface activity that we started with a spread instead of committing straight to the chunk.

The troll produced better than I expected for early August — three yellowfin in the 30 to 45 pound class came off a mixed spread of naked ballyhoo and small green-and-yellow Ilanders run off the shotgun and long riggers, plus a nice wahoo, low 40s, that grabbed a deep-diving lure run off a planer down the middle. Wahoo bites have been sporadic all summer out here, so getting one clean strike in daylight felt like a bonus rather than something to bank on. We lost a second wahoo bite to a bite-off on straight mono — should've had wire on that position from the jump, and that's on me. Lesson relearned: if the water's got that oily, warm look to it, wahoo are working the same seam as everything else, so rig for them even if you're targeting tuna.

White marlin showed too, and this is right on the clock for where we expected them. We flagged last week that the marlin bite would build through August rather than peak and fade, and that's exactly what we're seeing — three bites on dink ballyhoo behind small blue/white Sea Witches, two hookups, one release at the boat on a fish that came unglued at the last second on a circle hook that hadn't fully rotated. Nothing to complain about there. The marlin are following the same temperature edge as the tuna, working the current seam where the bait gets pinned against the drop.

Once the sun got up high and the troll bite went quiet — which it does out here by mid-morning once the light flattens the water — we shut down and set up to chunk over the drop past the 100-fathom curve, working the edge where it falls into 300, 400 fathom water off the southwest corner, what some of the Cape May boats call the Sled. Butterflied bunker chunks on straight 50s, no weight, letting it drift naturally down the current, put a bigeye in the box a little after dark — right around 90 pounds, came up slow and heavy on the second hook down, which is usually how they show themselves out here. Yellowfin kept picking at the chunk line through the night, nothing huge, mostly 25 to 35 pounders, but steady enough that we never really had a dead stretch. That matches what I said last week too — the yellowfin bite is steady rather than spectacular right now, holding right on that edge where the bait's riding the seam, not exploding in big pushes but reliable if you're patient and stay on the temp break instead of running around chasing birds.

Water on the inside of the break was running warmer than the open canyon water, which is typical for this time of year as the Stream throws off these filaments — you'll see it on the temp gauge before you see it on the surface, a jump of two, sometimes three degrees inside a quarter mile. That's the whole game out here in August: find where that warm tongue is laying against the canyon wall, and sit on it rather than running all over the numbers hoping for a bigger push.

What I'd do differently next trip: rig at least two positions with wire from the start given how active the wahoo have been on that seam, and I'd bring more bait for the chunk — we went through bunker faster than expected once the yellowfin got working under the boat after dark.

Looking ahead, if this high-pressure stretch holds like it's supposed to, I'd run the same play — troll the Elbow early, chunk the drop after dark — and I'd expect the white marlin numbers to keep building as we get deeper into August. The risk is the calendar: peak hurricane season is right around the corner, and one storm system spinning off the Stream can rearrange these filaments overnight. Until that happens, this is the pattern I'd fish, and the pattern I'd tell any of the other Indian River or Cape May boats to run too.
